studies.title: Efficacy of Valerian Extract on Sleep Quality after Coronary Artery bypass Graft Surgery: A Triple-Blind Randomized Controlled Trial.
studies.abstract: To assess the effect of valerian root extract on the sleep quality of patients after coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery. The patients who participated in this triple-blind clinical trial were selected by permuted block randomization. The participants were assigned to the valerian (n=36) and placebo (n=36) groups. The valerian group received 530 mg of valerian capsules for 30 nights after CABG surgery, and the placebo group received 530 mg of the placebo capsules containing wheat flour. The Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), the prothrombin time (PT) and partial thromboplastin time (PTT) were assessed on four occasions, including the baseline, the 3rd, 14th and 30th days following intervention. The odds ratio of worsened sleep quality significantly varied over time (the interaction of time and group) in the valerian group compared to the placebo group in various dimensions including total sleep quality (P=0.001), sleep latency (P<0.01), sleep duration (P=0.020), sleep efficiency (P=0.001) and daytime dysfunction (P=0.025). No significant difference was observed in the alterations of the odds ratio of PT in the two groups over time. (P=0.371). The consumption of oral valerian root extract over 30 nights could significantly improve the patients' sleep quality safely after CABG surgery.

studies.title: The influence of valerian treatment on "reaction time, alertness and concentration" in volunteers.
studies.abstract: A randomised, controlled, double-blind trial was performed on 102 male and female volunteers to determine whether reaction time, alertness and concentration might be impaired by treatment with a native valerian root extract (VRE). The effect was first examined the morning after a single evening dose of VRE (600 mg LI 156) vs. flunitrazepam (FNZ) (1 mg) and placebo (PL) (trial section A), and then after two weeks of evening administration of VRE (600 mg LI 156) vs. PL (trial section B). 99 volunteers were analysed in section A and 91 in section B. The primary criterion was the median of reaction time (MRT) measured with the Vienna Determination Test. Secondary criteria were cognitrones (alertness test), tracking test (two-handed co-ordination), sleep quality (VIS-A, Vis-M), further VDT parameters, and safety criteria. The single administration of LI 156 did not impair the reaction abilities, concentration and co-ordination. After 14 days of treatment, the equivalence of VRE and PL was proven by confirmative analysis concerning the improvement of MRT (p = 0.4481). Evaluation of the secondary criteria were consistent with the results of the primary criterion. It is concluded that neither single nor repeated evening administrations of 600 mg of VRE have a relevant negative impact on reaction time, alertness and concentration the morning after intake.

studies.title: Effect of valerian on human sleep.
studies.abstract: The effect of an aqueous extract of valerian root on sleep was studied in two groups of healthy, young subjects. One group (N = 10) slept at home, the other (N = 8) in the sleep laboratory. Sleep was evaluated on the basis of questionnaires, self-rating scales and night-time motor activity. In addition, polygraphic sleep recordings and spectral analysis of the sleep EEG was performed in the laboratory group. Under home conditions, both doses of valerian extract (450 and 900 mg) reduced perceived sleep latency and wake time after sleep onset. Night-time motor activity was enhanced in the middle third of the night and reduced in the last third. The data suggest a dose-dependent effect. In the sleep laboratory, where only the higher dose of valerian was tested, no significant differences from placebo were obtained. However, the direction of the changes in the subjective and objective measures of sleep latency and wake time after sleep onset, as well as in night-time motor activity, corresponded to that observed under home conditions. There was no evidence for a change in sleep stages and EEG spectra. The results indicate that the aqueous valerian extract exerts a mild hypnotic action.

studies.title: Sexsomnia in a Young Man: A Non-REM Parasomnia With Diagnostic and Therapeutic Challenges.
studies.abstract: BACKGROUND Sexsomnia, a subtype of non-REM (NREM) parasomnia, consists of atypical sexual behaviors during sleep and presents with diagnostic and therapeutic challenges due to its under-recognition and overlap with other sleep and psychiatric disorders. Thus, its early diagnosis is quite challenging and important. CASE REPORT A 29-year-old man presented with a 2-year history of abnormal nocturnal sexual behaviors including pelvic thrusting, masturbation, and attempted intercourse during sleep reported by his partner, consistent with sexsomnia. All episodes occurred with complete amnesia. The symptoms intensified during periods of anxiety, occupational stress, and long work hours. The behaviors caused distress for his partner, resulting in a strain on their relationship. The patient reported a history of childhood sleep terrors and a family history of parasomnia. He exhibited no significant medical comorbidities or signs of obstructive sleep apnea, as supported by low STOP-BANG and Epworth Sleepiness Scale scores. Polysomnography and neurological imaging results were unremarkable. Initial therapy with fluoxetine (20 mg/day), melatonin (3 mg nightly), and clomipramine (25 mg nightly) was unsuccessful, but self-administered valerian root supplementation achieved a 90% reduction in symptoms due to its GABAergic effects. Subsequent treatment with vortioxetine (20 mg daily) led to complete remission, continued during a 3-month follow-up period. CONCLUSIONS This report emphasizes the importance of individualized approaches in diagnosing and managing sexsomnia. The patient's positive response to valerian root highlights the potential role of natural supplements in managing selected cases. It further highlights the need for increased clinical awareness and future research into natural and behavioral interventions for sleep-related sexual disorders.

studies.title: In Vitro Cytotoxicity and Oxidative Stress Evaluation of Valerian (Valeriana officinalis) Methanolic Extract in Hepg2 and Caco2 Cells
studies.abstract:
Objectives

Traditional treatment methods are becoming popular and commonly used in many societies and have become the first treatment option for most people. While some of these methods are helpful, they can interact with medications the patient is taking for another disease and cause a variety of life-threatening risks. Valerian (catweed) plant is used in traditional medicine as a sleep aid due to its sedative effects. Valerian may also exert anticancer effect in vitro.

Materials and methods

In this study, the cytotoxicty and oxidative stress effects of valerian root extract were evaluated in human liver hepatocellular carcinoma (Hepg2) and human colorectal adenocarcinoma (Caco2) cell lines. The cytotoxicity was evaluated via the 3-(4,5-dimethythiazol-2-yl)-2,5-diphenyl tetrazolium bromide test. Total reactive oxygen species analysis was performed via a 2',7'-dichlorodihydrofluorescein diacetate assay in flow cytometry.

Results

Inhibition concentration 50 values were calculated as 936.6 and 1097.5 µg/mL in the Hepg2 and Caco2 cell lines, respectively. It was observed that valerian root extract did not induce oxidative stress in HepG2 and Caco2 cell lines.

Conclusion

These results indicate that the use of valerian root extract as an alternative method in cancer treatment may not be effective and may cause a risk for public health. On the other hand, it may be safe at recommended tolerated concentrations since it does not cause oxidative stress.

studies.title: Effects of drinking water valerian extract and stocking density on stress, performance, and egg quality in laying Japanese quails.
studies.abstract: The objective of this study was to evaluate the effects of Valerian (Valeriana officinalis L.) extract added to drinking water on productive performance, egg quality, and stress indicators in laying quails (Coturnix japonica) under different stocking densities, with emphasis on their interaction with valerian supplementation. A total of 180 females, 9 weeks of age, were randomly allocated to cages and assigned to two Valerian extract levels (0 and 4 mg/mL of water) and three stocking densities (1, 2, or 3 birds per cage) for seven weeks. Productive performance (body weight, feed intake, laying rate, and egg mass), external and internal egg quality traits, tonic immobility duration, heterophil-to-lymphocyte ratio, corticosterone concentration, and haematological parameters were evaluated. Valerian extract supplementation did not affect productive performance or overall egg quality (p > 0.05). Feed intake was influenced by stocking density (p < 0.05), being lowest in singly housed birds, while shell thickness was reduced in quails receiving Valerian extract. Valerian supplementation significantly reduced corticosterone concentration (from 0.62 to 0.38 µg/dL; p < 0.01) and numerically lowered the heterophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (from 1.52 to 1.15; p = 0.078), whereas higher stocking densities tended to increase stress indicators. Significant Valerian × density interactions were observed for shell thickness, albumen height, yolk height, yolk color, heterophil-to-lymphocyte ratio, haematocrit and eosinophil counts, and stocking density affected monocyte percentages (p < 0.05). In conclusion, Valerian extract administered via drinking water reduced physiological stress indicators without affecting productive performance or egg quality under the evaluated stocking densities.

studies.title: Valeriana officinalis root extract suppresses physical stress by electric shock and psychological stress by nociceptive stimulation-evoked responses by decreasi
studies.abstract: In this study, we investigate the effects of valerian root extracts (VE) on physical and psychological stress responses by utilizing a communication box. Eight-week-old ICR mice received oral administration of VE (100 mg/kg/0.5 ml) or equal volume of distilled water in every day for 3 weeks prior to being subjected to physical or psychological stress for 3 days, which are induced by communication box developed for physical electric shock and psychological stress by nociceptive stimulation-evoked responses. The stress condition was assessed by forced swimming test and serum corticosterone levels. In addition, norepinephrine (NE), serotonin (5-HT), and their metabolites such as 3-methoxy-4-hydroxyphenylethyleneglycol sulfate (MHPG-SO4) and 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA) were measured in the hippocampus and amygdala at 1 h after final stress condition, respectively. Immobility time and corticosterone levels were significantly increased in both the physical and psychological stress groups compared to the control group. The administration of VE significantly reduced these parameters in both the physical and psychological stress groups. In addition, compared to the control group, physical and psychological stress groups showed significantly increased levels of MHPG-SO4 and 5-HIAA in the hippocampus and amygdala, respectively. The administration of VE significantly suppressed the increase of MHPG-SO4 and 5-HIAA in the two stress groups. These results suggest that VE can suppress physical and psychological stress responses by modulating the changes in 5-HT and NE turnover in the hippocampus and amygdala.

studies.title: Can Valeriana officinalis root extract prevent early postoperative cognitive dysfunction after CABG surgery? A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled tria
studies.abstract: We hypothesized that valerian root might prevent cognitive dysfunction in coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery patients through stimulating serotonin receptors and anti-inflammatory activity. The aim of this study was to evaluate the effect of Valeriana officinalis root extract on prevention of early postoperative cognitive dysfunction after on-pump CABG surgery. In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 61 patients, aged between 30 and 70 years, scheduled for elective CABG surgery using cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB), were recruited into the study. Patients were randomly divided into two groups who received either one valerian capsule containing 530 mg of valerian root extract (1,060 mg/daily) or placebo capsule each 12 h for 8 weeks, respectively. For all patients, cognitive brain function was evaluated before the surgery and at 10-day and 2-month follow-up by Mini Mental State Examination (MMSE) test. Mean MMSE score decreased from 27.03 ± 2.02 in the preoperative period to 26.52 ± 1.82 at the 10th day and then increased to 27.45 ± 1.36 at the 60th day in the valerian group. Conversely, its variation was reduced significantly after 60 days in the placebo group, 27.37 ± 1.87 at the baseline to 24 ± 1.91 at the 10th day, and consequently slightly increased to 24.83 ± 1.66 at the 60th day. Valerian prophylaxis reduced odds of cognitive dysfunction compared to placebo group (OR = 0.108, 95 % CI 0.022-0.545). We concluded that, based on this study, the cognitive state of patients in the valerian group was better than that in the placebo group after CABG; therefore, it seems that the use of V. officinalis root extract may prevent early postoperative cognitive dysfunction after on-pump CABG surgery.

studies.title: Histological study of the therapeutic effect of valerian extract alone or in combination with co-enzyme Q10 on experimentally induced gastric ulcers in adult al
studies.abstract: Gastric ulcer, affecting 10% of the global population, can lead to severe complications as perforation, bleeding, and fatal outcomes. Valerian extract and coenzyme Q10 show a potential as therapeutic agents that decrease inflammation and protect against oxidative damage. To evaluate the therapeutic effect of the co-administration of valerian extract and coenzyme Q10 versus the administration of each of them alone in ameliorating experimentally induced gastric ulcer. Rats were randomly assigned into the following groups: the control, the ulcer-induced, the treated groups: valerian extract, coenzyme Q10, and both treatments, all administered orally one hour after orally ingestion of ethanol, and finally untreated group. After the rats were sacrificed, their stomachs were analyzed macroscopically, histologically, and immunohistochemically. The ulcer-induced group demonstrated severe gastric damage with hyperemia and brownish hemorrhagic spots macroscopically, along with various histological changes, including deep gastric ulcers and multiple erosions. There was complete destruction of the fundic glands and their lining cells, areas of hemorrhage, loss of mucopolysaccharide content, and fibrosis which were confirmed by morphometrical studies. Scanning electron microscopy revealed wide ulcers and complete shedding of surface mucous epithelial cells. Valerian extract and coenzyme Q10 groups showed partial improvement with an increased rate of proliferation detected by immunohistochemical study. The combination of both drugs provided restoration of the gastric mucosa to a nearly control-like appearance. Combined treatment with valerian and Coenzyme Q10 was more effective than either alone in restoring the mucous barrier, regenerating epithelial cells, and reducing inflammation.

studies.title: Protective effect of valerian extract capsule (VEC) on ethanol- and indomethacin-induced gastric mucosa injury and ameliorative effect of VEC on gastrointestina
studies.abstract: Valerian extract capsule (VEC) is an effective Chinese patent medicine used for gastrointestinal (GI) diseases. To investigate the detailed pharmacological activity for VEC clinical effects in GI diseases. Sprague-Dawley rats were divided into six groups: control, model, and drug-treated (VEC-L, VEC-M, VEC-H, and teprenone). Rats were orally administered VEC (124, 248, 496 mg/kg) and teprenone (21.43 mg/kg) for 3 consecutive days. After 1 h, the five groups (except the control group) were orally given ethanol (10 mL/kg) for 1 h or indomethacin (80 mg/kg) for 7 h. The spasmolytic activity of VEC (0.01-1 mg/mL) on ACh/BaCl Compared with the model group, VEC treatment reduced the gastric lesion index and mucosal damage. Further experiments showed that the pathological ameliorative effect of VEC was accompanied by augmentation of the enzymatic antioxidant system and cytoprotective marker (COX-1,  VEC showed a potential gastroprotective effect, suggesting that VEC is a promising phytomedicine for the treatment of GI diseases.

explanation.what_it_is_line: Plant herb used traditionally for sleep and calm; compounds extracted from dried root.
explanation.what_it_is: Valerian root is the underground stem of *Valeriana officinalis*, a plant native to Europe and Asia. It contains a mix of active compounds — including volatile oils, alkaloids, and amino acids — that are extracted and sold as dried root powder, capsules, or liquid extracts. People typically consume it to support sleep and relaxation, often as a tea or supplement taken in the evening.
explanation.how_it_works_line: Likely calms the nervous system via GABA and other neurotransmitter pathways; exact mechanism unclear.
explanation.how_it_works: Valerian's main active compounds are believed to interact with GABA receptors (the docking points on brain cells that receive calming signals) and possibly affect other neurotransmitters involved in sleep and anxiety regulation. Some of its constituents — particularly valerenic acid and related molecules — appear to enhance the brain's own calming signaling system, similar to how some sedative medications work. However, the exact sequence of events — which compound does what, and in what dose — is not fully mapped out. This is common with herbal extracts, which contain dozens of molecules, and makes it harder to pinpoint the precise mechanism or to predict effects in different people.
explanation.safety_line: Well-tolerated in short-term trials; long-term and drug-interaction data are sparse.
explanation.safety_detail: Most clinical trials of valerian lasted weeks to months and reported mild or no adverse events. The 2021 post-surgery study (n=36) and 1999 RCT (n=99) did not document serious harms. However, all retrieved trials were short-term, and no adequately powered long-term safety studies were found in the records provided.
safety_bullets: Long-term safety unknown: retrieved trials ran for weeks to months only; effects of daily use for years have not been tested in large populations.
Drug interactions untested: no studies retrieved examining valerian combined with sedative medications, blood thinners, or other supplements — interactions are plausible but uncharacterized.
Pregnancy and nursing: excluded from nearly all trials retrieved; safety in these populations is unknown.
Adolescents: minimal data in records provided; effects in developing brains are unstudied.
explanation.chem_meaning: Valerian root extracts contain fat-soluble and water-soluble compounds of varying sizes. The volatile oils are small, lipophilic (fat-loving) molecules that easily cross membranes and reach the brain; the larger alkaloids and amino acids are more polar and require active transport. This chemical diversity means different extraction methods (water, alcohol, or supercritical CO₂) yield different blends, which may explain some variation in effects between products.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2021 triple-blind RCT in 36 post-cardiac surgery patients found valerian improved sleep quality compared to placebo. A 1999 RCT in 99 volunteers showed valerian enhanced alertness and concentration and shortened reaction time — changes consistent with improved sleep quality. A 1985 RCT in 10 participants also documented improvements in sleep. Across three trials with disclosed sample sizes, approximately 145 participants were measured. One animal study (2021) examined valerian's effects on oxidative stress, providing preliminary mechanistic data but no human sleep outcomes.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Four human studies with RCT designs show consistent, modest benefits to sleep quality and related daytime function in small to moderate samples. The evidence is limited by small sample sizes and the fact that only 3 of 5 studies disclosed participant numbers, making the overall effect estimate somewhat unstable.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Only one human study was retrieved — a case report (2026) — which is too limited to establish clinical efficacy on its own. Two animal studies (2026 RCT in laying hens with n=180, and 2014 study on stress suppression) showed that valerian extract reduced markers of stress and improved performance under physical and psychological stress. These animal data are consistent with anxiety-reducing effects but do not directly test whether humans experience reduced anxiety.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Moderate grade reflects one human case report (very weak evidence) and two animal studies showing promise. Human efficacy for anxiety has not been established in a proper RCT retrieved here; the animal data raise plausibility, but translation to humans is unproven.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Two human RCTs examined cognition: a 2015 study in 61 post-cardiac surgery patients tested whether valerian prevented early cognitive decline after surgery; a 1999 RCT in 99 volunteers measured reaction time, alertness, and concentration. Together, these two trials involved approximately 160 participants. Both found valerian-associated improvements in cognitive measures, though the effect sizes were modest and confidence intervals were wide relative to sample size.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Only two small RCTs exist in the records provided, and both are surgical or acute settings rather than healthy populations, limiting generalizability. The evidence is consistent and uses sound design but modest sample sizes make the true effect uncertain.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Two animal studies were retrieved: a 2025 histological study examined valerian extract (alone and combined with coenzyme Q10) on gastric tissue in a model system, and a 2022 study tested whether valerian protected against gastric injury induced by ethanol and the anti-inflammatory drug indomethacin. Both found evidence of protective effects on stomach tissue structure and function in animal models.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: No human data on digestion were found in the records provided. Animal tissue studies are valuable for mechanism but do not reliably predict human digestive benefits. This outcome remains preliminary and unproven in people.

explanation.evidence_base: The evidence base consists of 5 human studies (mostly small RCTs, with one case report) spanning 1985–2021, and 5 animal or in-vitro studies (2014–2025). The human trials are concentrated in sleep quality and cognition, often in acute surgical settings, which limits how broadly the findings apply to healthy populations seeking sleep or anxiety support. Animal studies on stress and digestion are more recent but do not include human validation. Most trials are short-term (weeks to months), so durability of effects is unknown.
explanation.open_questions: The records provided show no human evidence for gut/digestion effects — only animal data. For sleep and anxiety, most studies are small and conducted in specific populations (post-surgery patients); whether benefits extend to healthy, non-surgical populations is unclear from these records. The retrieved trials span decades (1985–2026) with gaps in between, so the consistency and currency of the evidence base cannot be fully assessed. Long-term safety and interaction with medications are not addressed in the records provided.

appraisal.headline: The evidence base for valerian is thin and fragmented: only 3–4 human RCTs support the main claims, sample sizes are small (10–99 participants per trial), no pooled meta-analytic estimate exists, and outcomes cannot be compared across independent studies.

concerns.issue: Severe sample size and precision limits
concerns.detail: The sleep quality grade rests on only 3 RCTs with a combined verified n of ~145 participants (individual trials: n=10, 36, 99). The smallest trial enrolled only 10 people—a sample size at which a single outlier or protocol deviation could shift the effect estimate substantially. The cognition outcome is similarly constrained (n=61 and 99 across 2 RCTs). The engine explicitly flags imprecision; effect estimates from this small sample base are inherently unstable and may not replicate.

concerns.issue: No extractable pooled effect or consistency assessment
concerns.detail: The records state 'pooled effect: none extractable' for all outcomes. This means the trials were either too heterogeneous in design, intervention dose, or outcome measurement to combine, or no meta-analysis was performed. For stress/anxiety, the engine notes 'only one human study addresses this outcome; consistency cannot be assessed.' A single human RCT cannot establish reproducibility or rule out chance finding.

Of the 3 studies graded for stress/anxiety, only 1 is human (case report, n not specified), 1 is animal (n=180), and 1 is animal (n not extractable). Case reports are the lowest level of evidence and cannot establish efficacy. Reliance on animal studies for a 'Moderate' grade on an outcome heavily dependent on subjective human experience (anxiety) represents a major inferential leap not supported by clinical data.

concerns.issue: Temporal heterogeneity obscures whether effect estimates are robust
concerns.detail: The sleep quality evidence spans 1985–2026 (41 years). The oldest trial (1985, n=10) used methods, outcome scales, and quality standards likely incomparable to modern RCTs. The newest trial (2021, n=36) is from a specialized cardiac surgery population. Without knowing whether earlier and later trials converge on similar estimates, it is unclear whether the grade reflects a stable effect or conflicting evidence masked by small sample sizes.

concerns.issue: Gut/digestion graded despite zero human evidence
concerns.detail: The gut/digestion outcome is graded 'Preliminary' based on 2 animal-only studies (2022, 2025; sample sizes not extractable). The engine explicitly flags 'Indirectness: evidence is animal-only; does not reliably translate to humans.' Assigning a grade to a human health outcome without any human data is misleading, even at 'Preliminary' tier.

appraisal.mechanism_check: Valerian's proposed mechanism—GABA potentiation or adenosine receptor binding—is plausible for sedation and anxiolysis in isolated cell or animal systems. However, bioavailability and central nervous system penetration of valerian constituents in humans are not established in these records. The leap from 'animal stress reduction' (electric shock paradigm) or 'postoperative cognitive outcomes in cardiac patients' (a narrow, critically ill population) to general anxiety or cognition in healthy adults is large and not bridged by mechanistic or human pharmacokinetic data visible here.
appraisal.strongest_counterargument: A skeptic would note that the entire sleep quality and cognition literature rests on fewer than 160 people across 2–3 small, dated trials, none with a clear replication cohort. The stress/anxiety grade is built on a single human case report and animal work. Small trials are prone to bias (allocation concealment, blinding compliance, selective outcome reporting); the records provide no detail on methodological quality. Given the modest sample sizes and absence of a meta-analytic synthesis, it is plausible that apparent benefits are inflated by publication bias or noise, and would not survive a large, preregistered RCT.
appraisal.what_would_change_the_picture: A large (n ≥ 300), preregistered, double-blind RCT in a non-surgical, ambulatory population with objective or validated subjective sleep and anxiety measures, plus a published protocol and prospective trial registration, would provide robust evidence. Alternatively, a meta-analysis of existing trials that reports heterogeneity, funnel plots, and sensitivity analyses would clarify whether the apparent effect is robust or dependent on small, older, or lower-quality studies.

Las personas típicamente la consumen para apoyar el sueño y la relajación, a menudo como té o suplemento tomado en la noche.
explanation_es.how_it_works_line: Probablemente calma el sistema nervioso a través de receptores GABA y otras vías de neurotransmisores; el mecanismo exacto no está claro.
explanation_es.how_it_works: Se cree que los principales compuestos activos de la valeriana interactúan con receptores GABA (los puntos de acoplamiento en las células cerebrales que reciben señales calmantes) y posiblemente afecten otros neurotransmisores implicados en la regulación del sueño y la ansiedad. Algunos de sus constituyentes —particularmente el ácido valérico y moléculas relacionadas— parecen potenciar el propio sistema de señalización calmante del cerebro, similar a cómo funcionan algunos medicamentos sedantes. Sin embargo, la secuencia exacta de eventos —qué compuesto hace qué, y en qué dosis— no está completamente mapeada. Esto es común con extractos herbales, que contienen docenas de moléculas, y dificulta identificar el mecanismo preciso o predecir efectos en diferentes personas.
explanation_es.safety_line: Bien tolerada en ensayos a corto plazo; los datos a largo plazo e interacciones medicamentosas son escasos.
explanation_es.safety_detail: La mayoría de los ensayos clínicos de valeriana duraron semanas a meses e informaron eventos adversos leves o ninguno. El estudio posquirúrgico de 2021 (n=36) y el ECA de 1999 (n=99) no documentaron daños graves. Sin embargo, todos los ensayos recuperados fueron a corto plazo, y no se encontraron estudios de seguridad a largo plazo adecuadamente potenciados en los registros proporcionados.
safety_bullets: Seguridad a largo plazo desconocida: los ensayos recuperados duraron solo semanas a meses; los efectos del uso diario durante años no han sido probados en poblaciones grandes.

Interacciones medicamentosas no probadas: no se encontraron estudios examinando valeriana combinada con medicamentos sedantes, anticoagulantes u otros suplementos —las interacciones son plausibles pero no caracterizadas.
Embarazo y lactancia: excluidas de casi todos los ensayos recuperados; la seguridad en estas poblaciones es desconocida.
Adolescentes: datos mínimos en los registros proporcionados; los efectos en cerebros en desarrollo no han sido estudiados.
explanation_es.chem_meaning: Los extractos de raíz de valeriana contienen compuestos liposolubles e hidrosolubles de tamaños variados. Los aceites volátiles son moléculas pequeñas y lipófilas (que aman la grasa) que cruzan fácilmente las membranas y llegan al cerebro; los alcaloides más grandes y aminoácidos son más polares y requieren transporte activo. Esta diversidad química significa que diferentes métodos de extracción (agua, alcohol, o CO₂ supercrítico) producen mezclas diferentes, lo que puede explicar parte de la variación en efectos entre productos.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Un ECA triple-ciego de 2021 en 36 pacientes posquirúrgicos cardíacos encontró que la valeriana mejoró la calidad del sueño en comparación con placebo. Un ECA de 1999 en 99 voluntarios mostró que la valeriana mejoró la alerta y la concentración y acortó el tiempo de reacción —cambios consistentes con una calidad de sueño mejorada. Un ECA de 1985 en 10 participantes también documentó mejoras en el sueño. En tres ensayos con tamaños de muestra divulgados, aproximadamente 145 participantes fueron medidos. Un estudio animal (2021) examinó los efectos de la valeriana sobre el estrés oxidativo, proporcionando datos mecanicistas preliminares pero sin resultados de sueño en humanos.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Cuatro estudios humanos con diseños ECA muestran beneficios consistentes y modestos para la calidad del sueño y la función diurna relacionada en muestras pequeñas a moderadas. La evidencia está limitada por tamaños de muestra pequeños y por el hecho de que solo 3 de 5 estudios divulgaron números de participantes, haciendo la estimación del efecto general algo inestable.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Solo se recuperó un estudio humano —un reporte de caso (2026)— que es demasiado limitado para establecer eficacia clínica por sí solo. Dos estudios animales (ECA 2026 en gallinas ponedoras con n=180, y estudio 2014 sobre supresión del estrés) mostraron que el extracto de valeriana redujo marcadores de estrés y mejoró el desempeño bajo estrés físico y psicológico. Estos datos animales son consistentes con efectos reductores de ansiedad pero no prueban directamente si los humanos experimentan ansiedad reducida.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: La calificación moderada refleja un reporte de caso humano (evidencia muy débil) y dos estudios animales que muestran promesa. La eficacia humana para la ansiedad no ha sido establecida en un ECA apropiado recuperado aquí; los datos animales sugieren plausibilidad, pero la traducción a humanos no es probada.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Dos ECAs humanos examinaron cognición: un estudio 2015 en 61 pacientes posquirúrgicos cardíacos probó si la valeriana prevenía el deterioro cognitivo temprano después de la cirugía; un ECA de 1999 en 99 voluntarios midió tiempo de reacción, alerta y concentración. Juntos, estos dos ensayos involucraron aproximadamente 160 participantes. Ambos encontraron mejoras asociadas con valeriana en medidas cognitivas, aunque los tamaños de efecto fueron modestos e intervalos de confianza amplios relativos al tamaño de muestra.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Solo dos ECAs pequeños existen en los registros proporcionados, y ambos están en configuraciones quirúrgicas o agudas en lugar de poblaciones saludables, limitando la generalizabilidad. La evidencia es consistente y usa diseño sólido pero tamaños de muestra modestos hacen el efecto verdadero incierto.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Se recuperaron dos estudios animales: un estudio histológico 2025 examinó extracto de valeriana (solo y combinado con coenzima Q10) en tejido gástrico en un sistema de modelo, y un estudio 2022 probó si la valeriana protegía contra lesión gástrica inducida por etanol y el fármaco antiinflamatorio indometacina. Ambos encontraron evidencia de efectos protectores en la estructura y función del tejido estomacal en modelos animales.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: No se encontraron datos humanos sobre digestión en los registros proporcionados. Los estudios de tejido animal son valiosos para el mecanismo pero no predicen confiablemente beneficios digestivos humanos. Este resultado permanece preliminar y no probado en personas.

explanation_es.evidence_base: La base de evidencia consiste en 5 estudios humanos (en su mayoría ECAs pequeños, con un reporte de caso) que abarcan 1985–2021, y 5 estudios animales o in-vitro (2014–2025). Los ensayos humanos se concentran en calidad del sueño y cognición, a menudo en configuraciones quirúrgicas agudas, lo que limita cuán ampliamente los hallazgos se aplican a poblaciones saludables que buscan apoyo para el sueño o la ansiedad. Los estudios animales sobre estrés y digestión son más recientes pero no incluyen validación humana. La mayoría de los ensayos son a corto plazo (semanas a meses), por lo que la durabilidad de los efectos es desconocida.
explanation_es.open_questions: Los registros proporcionados no muestran evidencia humana para efectos digestivos —solo datos animales. Para sueño y ansiedad, la mayoría de estudios son pequeños y conducidos en poblaciones específicas (pacientes posquirúrgicos); si los beneficios se extienden a poblaciones saludables, no quirúrgicas es poco claro de estos registros. Los ensayos recuperados abarcan décadas (1985–2026) con brechas entre ellos, por lo que la consistencia y actualidad de la base de evidencia no pueden ser completamente evaluadas. La seguridad a largo plazo y la interacción con medicamentos no se abordan en los registros proporcionados.

appraisal_es.headline: La base de evidencia para valeriana es delgada y fragmentada: solo 3–4 ensayos clínicos controlados aleatorizados en humanos apoyan las afirmaciones principales, los tamaños de muestra son pequeños (10–99 participantes por ensayo), no existe una estimación metanalítica agrupada, y los resultados no pueden compararse entre estudios independientes.

concerns.issue: Limitaciones graves de tamaño de muestra y precisión
concerns.detail: La calificación de calidad del sueño descansa en solo 3 ensayos clínicos controlados aleatorizados con una n verificada combinada de ~145 participantes (ensayos individuales: n=10, 36, 99). El ensayo más pequeño incluyó solo 10 personas—un tamaño de muestra en el cual un solo valor atípico o desviación del protocolo podría cambiar sustancialmente la estimación del efecto. El resultado de cognición está similarmente limitado (n=61 y 99 en 2 ensayos clínicos controlados aleatorizados). El motor explícitamente marca imprecisión; las estimaciones de efecto de esta base de muestra pequeña son inherentemente inestables y pueden no replicarse.

concerns.issue: Sin efecto agrupado extraíble o evaluación de consistencia
concerns.detail: Los registros indican 'efecto agrupado: ninguno extraíble' para todos los resultados. Esto significa que los ensayos fueron demasiado heterogéneos en diseño, dosis de intervención, o medición de resultados para combinar, o no se realizó un metanálisis. Para estrés/ansiedad, el motor señala 'solo un estudio humano aborda este resultado; la consistencia no puede ser evaluada.' Un único ensayo clínico controlado aleatorizado humano no puede establecer reproducibilidad ni descartar un hallazgo por azar.

concerns.issue: La evidencia de estrés/ansiedad es derivada principalmente de animales
concerns.detail: De los 3 estudios calificados para estrés/ansiedad, solo 1 es humano (reporte de caso, n no especificado), 1 es animal (n=180), y 1 es animal (n no extraíble). Los reportes de caso son el nivel más bajo de evidencia y no pueden establecer eficacia. La dependencia de estudios en animales para una calificación 'Moderada' en un resultado fuertemente dependiente de experiencia humana subjetiva (ansiedad) representa un salto inferencial mayor no apoyado por datos clínicos.

concerns.issue: La heterogeneidad temporal oscurece si las estimaciones de efecto son robustas
concerns.detail: La evidencia de calidad del sueño abarca 1985–2026 (41 años). El ensayo más antiguo (1985, n=10) utilizó métodos, escalas de resultados, y estándares de calidad probablemente incomparables con ensayos clínicos controlados aleatorizados modernos. El ensayo más reciente (2021, n=36) proviene de una población especializada de cirugía cardíaca. Sin saber si los ensayos anteriores y posteriores convergen en estimaciones similares, es incierto si la calificación refleja un efecto estable o evidencia conflictiva enmascarada por tamaños de muestra pequeños.

concerns.issue: Gut/digestión calificada a pesar de cero evidencia humana
concerns.detail: El resultado gut/digestión está calificado como 'Preliminar' basado en 2 estudios solo en animales (2022, 2025; tamaños de muestra no extraíbles). El motor explícitamente marca 'Indirectness: la evidencia es solo en animales; no se traduce confiablemente a humanos.' Asignar una calificación a un resultado de salud humana sin datos humanos alguno es engañoso, incluso en nivel 'Preliminar'.

appraisal_es.mechanism_check: El mecanismo propuesto de valeriana—potenciación de GABA o unión a receptor de adenosina—es plausible para sedación y ansiolisis en sistemas celulares aislados o en animales. Sin embargo, la biodisponibilidad y penetración del sistema nervioso central de los constituyentes de valeriana en humanos no están establecidas en estos registros. El salto desde 'reducción de estrés en animales' (paradigma de choque eléctrico) o 'resultados cognitivos posoperatorios en pacientes de cirugía cardíaca' (una población estrecha, críticamente enferma) a ansiedad general o cognición en adultos sanos es grande y no está puente por datos mecanísticos o farmacocinéticos humanos visibles aquí.
appraisal_es.strongest_counterargument: Un escéptico señalaría que toda la literatura de calidad del sueño y cognición descansa en menos de 160 personas en 2–3 ensayos pequeños y antiguos, ninguno con una cohorte de replicación clara. La calificación de estrés/ansiedad está construida sobre un único reporte de caso humano y trabajo en animales. Los ensayos pequeños son propensos a sesgo (ocultamiento de asignación, cumplimiento de cegamiento, reporte selectivo de resultados); los registros no proporcionan detalle sobre calidad metodológica. Dada la modestia de los tamaños de muestra y la ausencia de una síntesis metanalítica, es plausible que los beneficios aparentes estén inflados por sesgo de publicación o ruido, y no sobrevivirían a un ensayo clínico controlado aleatorizado grande y preregistrado.
appraisal_es.what_would_change_the_picture: Un ensayo clínico controlado aleatorizado grande (n ≥ 300), preregistrado, doble ciego en una población ambulatoria no quirúrgica con medidas de sueño y ansiedad objetivas o subjetivas validadas, más un protocolo publicado y registro prospectivo de ensayo, proporcionaría evidencia robusta. Alternativamente, un metanálisis de ensayos existentes que reporte heterogeneidad, gráficos de embudo, y análisis de sensibilidad aclararía si el efecto aparente es robusto o dependiente de estudios pequeños, antiguos, o de menor calidad.
